content: N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide, commonly referred to as DEET, is a slightly yellow, oily substance that serves as the most widely used active ingredient in insect repellents. It is designed for application on the skin or clothing to protect against a variety of biting insects, including mosquitoes, ticks, fleas, chiggers, and leeches. DEET was originally developed by the United States Army after its experiences with jungle warfare during World War II. Initially tested as a pesticide for agricultural use, it was introduced for military use in 1946 and became available for civilian use in 1957. It was extensively used during the Vietnam War and in other regions of Southeast Asia. At room temperature, DEET exists as a slightly yellow liquid. It can be synthesized by converting m-toluic acid (3-methylbenzoic acid) into its corresponding acyl chloride, which is then reacted with diethylamine. Historically, DEET was thought to function by blocking insect olfactory receptors that detect 1-octen-3-ol, a volatile compound found in human sweat and breath. This mechanism was believed to blind insects to the presence of humans or animals, thereby preventing their feeding behavior. However, it has since been determined that DEET acts as a true repellent, as mosquitoes strongly dislike its odor. Specific olfactory receptor neurons in mosquito antennae, which are activated by DEET and other repellents like eucalyptol, linalool, and thujone, have been identified. Behavioral studies have shown that DEET effectively repels mosquitoes even in the absence of body odor attractants such as 1-octen-3-ol, lactic acid, or carbon dioxide. Both male and female mosquitoes exhibit the same aversion to DEET. Recent structural studies have revealed that DEET binds with high specificity to Anopheles gambiae odorant binding protein 1 (AgamOBP1), suggesting that this protein may be a molecular target for DEET and other repellents. This finding has significant implications for evaluating the long-term effectiveness of repellents. A conserved protein in the ionotropic receptor family, IR40a, has been identified as a potential DEET receptor in the antennae of flies. Neurons expressing IR40a respond to DEET in an IR40a-dependent manner, and flies lacking IR40a lose their avoidance behavior toward DEET vapors. Structurally related repellents also activate this receptor, suggesting its utility in screening for new repellents. However, studies in the southern house mosquito (Culex quinquefasciatus) have shown that reducing IR40a transcript levels does not affect DEET-induced behavior or electrophysiological responses, indicating that IR40a is not involved in DEET reception in this species. Instead, another receptor, CquiOR136, has been identified as responsible for DEET detection in Culex mosquitoes. Knockdown experiments targeting CquiOR136 significantly reduced electrophysiological responses to DEET and eliminated behavioral repulsion, confirming its role in DEET reception. DEET is commonly available in spray or lotion formulations, with concentrations ranging up to 100%. Higher concentrations correlate with longer durations of protection against insect bites. For example, 100% DEET provides up to 12 hours of protection, while formulations containing 20-34% DEET offer 3-6 hours of protection. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends using products with 30-50% DEET to prevent the transmission of insect-borne diseases. Manufacturers advise against applying DEET under clothing or on damaged skin and recommend washing it off after use. DEET can act as an irritant and, in rare cases, may cause severe skin reactions. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has documented 14 to 46 cases of potential DEET-associated seizures, including four fatalities, but notes that the seizure rate is extremely low, at approximately one per 100 million users. The American Academy of Pediatrics considers DEET concentrations of 10-30% safe for use in children and adults but advises against its use on infants under two months old. Health Canada has restricted the sale of DEET products with concentrations exceeding 30% and recommends limited use in children, with specific guidelines for frequency and concentration based on age. DEET is a potent solvent and can dissolve certain plastics, synthetic fabrics like rayon and spandex, and painted or varnished surfaces, including nail polish. Environmentally, DEET does not bioaccumulate but exhibits slight toxicity to coldwater fish such as rainbow trout and tilapia, as well as some freshwater zooplankton species. Trace amounts of DEET have been detected in water bodies, including the Mississippi River and its tributaries, with concentrations ranging from 5 to 201 ng/L in a 1991 study.
